_purpose: Researcher-facing overview of this package. Points into source/evidence.json for provenance, materials/materials.json for participant-visible content, and task/ + evaluation/ for the runnable contract.

paper.title: Analyzing Frictions in Generalized Second-Price Auction Markets
paper.venue: Information Systems Research, Vol. 34, No. 4, December 2023, pp. 1437-1454

external_sources_policy_note: No OSF or open-materials URL was supplied by the contributor for this job. Per the package-builder's opt-in policy, no web search, web fetch, DOI resolution, or repository/author-page discovery was performed. This entire package is built from input/paper.pdf only. The paper's own online appendix (referenced repeatedly in-text as Online Appendices A-N) was therefore NOT retrieved; see audit/missing_information.json for every place this leaves a gap.

empirical_studies.name: Agent-based Q-learning simulation of the GSP environment with bid-adjustment frictions
empirical_studies.sample: 100,000 simulated runs of M=2,000 matches x T=100 periods per match, J=3 Q-learning agents per match competing for K=2 ad slots
empirical_studies.conditions: Full factorial C in {0.0, 0.5, 1.0} x alpha in {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}
key_findings: Result 1: lower bid-adjustment costs lead to more exploration (more bid adjustments).
Result 2: bid-to-value ratio is higher for lower-valued agents.
Result 3: for the lowest-valued agents, bid-to-value ratio increases as friction decreases.
Result 4: bid-to-value ratio decreases as alpha increases.
Result 5: allocative efficiency of the market increases as friction costs increase.
empirical_studies.role_in_package: Supplies the GSP environment/payoff formulas that task/adapter.py reuses; not itself modeled as a runnable human-study task.

empirical_studies.name: Main laboratory human-subject experiment
empirical_studies.sample: 138 participants, 8 lab sessions of 15-18 participants each, recruited via ORSEE at Purdue University
empirical_studies.conditions: Between-subjects: bid-adjustment cost C in {0.0 (costless), 0.1 (costly)}. Within-subjects: alpha (slot-2/slot-1 value ratio) in {0.2 (low), 0.5 (medium), 0.8 (high)}. 10 matches per session, groups of J=3 re-randomized each match.
empirical_studies.participant_flow: Handout instructions read aloud -> 6 sequential practice tasks (must pass to advance) -> 5 randomized worked examples -> 10 real paid matches (continuous-time bidding within each match, silent mouse-based bid revision, random termination, single randomly-drawn-period payment) -> cash payment.
outcomes_measured: Number of bid adjustments per participant per match (exploration), by value rank
Bid-to-value ratio (Omega_j = bid/value) per participant per match, by value rank
Allocative efficiency (Psi) of the match (realized welfare / max possible welfare), by treatment
key_findings: Result 6: bid adjustments are an order of magnitude higher at C=0.0 than C=0.1; lowest-valued participants adjust most.
Result 7: lowest-valued participants substantially overbid relative to others.
Result 8: lowest-valued participants' bid-to-value ratio is significantly higher at C=0.0 than C=0.1.
Result 9: bid-to-value ratio decreases as alpha increases, for medium/highest-valued participants (partial support for the analogous computational result).
Result 10: allocative efficiency is significantly higher at C=0.1 (0.98) than C=0.0 (0.94).
empirical_studies.role_in_package: Primary human-subject study modeled by task/task.json + task/adapter.py (condition set 'human_main').

empirical_studies.name: Discrete-time / information-cost follow-up experiment ('Experiment to Study the Underlying Mechanism')
empirical_studies.sample: 183 new participants (no overlap with human_main), recruited at Purdue University, programmed in oTree
empirical_studies.conditions: 2x2 factorial: bid-adjustment cost C in {0.0, 0.1} x counterfactual-information cost in {free, $0.5/period}. Alpha fixed at 0.5 for all four cells (not varied). Discrete-time decision periods (expected 10 per match, termination probability 0.1/period) instead of continuous time; private values drawn independently each match (not matched across groups/treatments as in human_main's later matches).
empirical_studies.participant_flow: oTree-based instructions and decision screens (Online Appendix N.1, not available in this PDF) -> repeated matches with discrete decision periods, optional purchase of a counterfactual-payoff plot each period depending on treatment -> payment.
outcomes_measured: Number of bid adjustments per participant per match, by value rank and treatment cell
Bid-to-value ratio per participant per match, by value rank and treatment cell
Allocative efficiency of the match, by treatment cell
key_findings: Bid adjustments are significantly higher when C=0.0 than C=0.1, and higher when information is costly than when it is free.

Lowest-valued participants again show the highest bid-to-value ratio, especially with costly information and no bid-adjustment cost; bid-adjustment costs substantially mitigate this overbidding when information is costly.
Allocative efficiency improves with bid-adjustment costs in both the free- and costly-information conditions (weaker significance in the free-information condition).
empirical_studies.role_in_package: Second human-subject study; modeled by task/task.json + task/adapter.py (condition set 'human_mechanism').

empirical_studies.name: Additional calibrated computational simulations
empirical_studies.sample: Computational simulations, Q-learning parameters (delta, lambda) calibrated to human_main data
empirical_studies.conditions: (a) Lowest-valued agent restricted to never overbid (b3<=v3), alpha=0.5, C=0.5, J=3, K=2. (b) Number of advertisers J varied over {3,4,5,6}, alpha=0.5, C=0.5, K=2.
key_findings: (a) Restricting the lowest-valued agent from overbidding raises allocative efficiency from 0.951 to 0.958 (~5% of the relevant range).

(b) As the number of advertisers increases, allocative efficiency decreases, lowest-valued agents overbid more, and this cascades into higher-valued advertisers' bids; the core friction-increases-efficiency result holds across market sizes.
empirical_studies.role_in_package: Context/robustness only; not implemented as a runnable task (no new human-subject data).

package_entry_point.example_full_run: python3 task/adapter.py --study human_main --cost 0.1 --alpha 0.5 --num-matches 10 --agent-policy truthful --seed 1 --output run.json && python3 evaluation/evaluation.py run.json

readiness_status.summary: task/adapter.py runs fully offline, implements both human-subject studies' condition sets and the paper's own GSP payoff formulas, and passes --smoke-test. It cannot reproduce the paper's exact continuous-time UI, the verbatim instructions handouts, or its cross-session inferential statistics (bootstrapped SEs / permutation tests), because those depend on materials or raw session data not present in the uploaded PDF and not authorized for external retrieval on this job. See audit/missing_information.json for the itemized list (AUD-01 through AUD-10) and task/task.json#derived_design_decisions for the specific simplifications made to keep the task runnable.
